title: One Building on Mountain Avenue: Unix, C, and a Degree Never Collected
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Bronxville and Summit, a Switching Engineer's House

stops.name: Bronxville, birth in a Bell Labs family
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the place is reconstruction. No source names the hospital, and the research pool's own note concedes the hospital was inferred from the family's residence. Anchored on Bronxville village.
stops.campa: Dennis MacAlistair Ritchie is born in Bronxville, in Westchester County, to Alistair E. Ritchie and Jean McGee Ritchie. The father is a Bell Telephone Laboratories man, a switching-systems engineer whose working life is spent on the apparatus that lets one telephone find another across a continent. In that house relays and circuits and switching logic are ordinary domestic vocabulary. He will end at his father's company, in his father's state, working one layer up on a version of the same problem. No source names the hospital.
suggested_refs: Alistair E. Ritchie's published work on switching circuit theory at Bell Telephone Laboratories

stops.name: Summit, the move across the state line
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: sources date the move only to 'the 1940s' with no year. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The family leaves Westchester for Summit, New Jersey, a commuter town in Union County within easy reach of the Bell Labs campuses where Alistair Ritchie works. Dennis grows up here. Summit sits about seven miles from Murray Hill, where the company is consolidating its research operation into a long low building on Mountain Avenue. The boy will make that seven-mile trip, in one direction or the other, for most of the next sixty years. As an adult he changes address once, by four miles, inside the same county.
suggested_refs: The Bell Telephone Laboratories campus at 600 Mountain Avenue, Murray Hill, seven miles from the Ritchie house

stops.name: Summit High School, the line in the obituaries
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the graduation is attested, the year is not. Inferred from Harvard matriculation in 1959; month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates corrected to the school at 125 Kent Place Boulevard, against the research pool's value, which fell in downtown Summit.
stops.campa: Ritchie attends the public high school of Summit, on Kent Place Boulevard, and graduates from it. Nothing in the reachable record describes what he studied there, what he was like, or who taught him. The school appears in the obituaries as a single line laid between the name of the town and the name of Harvard, and the men who later wrote about him at length, Kernighan and Pike and McIlroy, all met him a decade after he left it. He leaves for Cambridge in 1959 to read physics.
suggested_refs: Summit High School, 125 Kent Place Boulevard, Summit, New Jersey

segments.name: Harvard, and a Degree Never Collected

stops.name: Harvard Yard, matriculation in physics
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month is the ordinary start of the Harvard academic year and is not separately sourced.
stops.campa: Ritchie enters Harvard to read physics. The field is at its post-war height, and the applied mathematics sitting beside it is acquiring a new subject matter: what a computation is, what it costs, which problems admit one at all. He drifts toward that second track without leaving the first. Harvard has no computer science department to drift into. The machines live in the Computation Laboratory; the theory sits inside the mathematics of engineering, in a division that also teaches applied physics.
suggested_refs: The Harvard Computation Laboratory and the Division of Engineering and Applied Physics, c. 1959

stops.name: Harvard Yard, the degrees in physics and applied mathematics
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is the ordinary Harvard commencement and is not separately sourced.
stops.campa: He takes his degree in physics with applied mathematics behind it, and stays on. Nobody graduates in computer science in 1963, because the discipline has not been assembled yet. Ritchie's formal training is in the physical sciences and in the mathematics of what a machine can be made to do: how long a computation takes, how much of a machine it occupies, whether it can be done at all. He does not write a program that anyone outside a university has to read for another nine years.
suggested_refs: ACM A.M. Turing Award biographical citation, which records the Harvard degrees

stops.name: Pierce Hall, the thesis under Patrick Fischer
stops.date_confidence: the supervision and subject are attested for 1963; the building is reconstruction. No source places Ritchie's graduate work in any named Harvard building. Fischer's appointment was in applied mathematics, in the Division of Engineering and Applied Physics, which makes Pierce Hall and the Aiken Computation Laboratory the defensible anchor; the research pool's Lyman Laboratory of Physics is not.
stops.campa: He begins doctoral work under Patrick C. Fischer, an assistant professor in the Division of Engineering and Applied Physics, on computational complexity and recursive function theory. The thesis takes shape as Program Structure and Computational Complexity, an argument about the cost of computation carried out on paper, in a university that keeps its computing inside an engineering building rather than in a department of its own. Ritchie is twenty-two and has not yet worked on a machine that anybody else depends on.
suggested_refs: Pierce Hall and the Aiken Computation Laboratory, Oxford Street, Harvard University

stops.name: Harvard, the dissertation finished and the degree left
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01. No reachable source explains why the degree was never conferred.
stops.campa: The dissertation is finished and Ritchie does not formally receive the degree. By 1968 he has been employed at Bell Labs for a year and is working on an operating system that will not exist for another eighteen months; the piece of paper is not needed by anyone, least of all by him. The typescript passes into private hands and stays there for more than half a century, until the Computer History Museum acquires a copy and digitizes it. He never used the title.
suggested_refs: Program Structure and Computational Complexity, Harvard dissertation, 1968, Computer History Museum accession 102784979
sources: Computer History Museum, 2020 acquisition and digitization of the thesis

segments.name: Murray Hill: the Withdrawal and the Spare Machine

stops.name: Murray Hill, the Computing Science Research Center
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the canonical atlas Murray Hill pin, inherited unchanged; Wikipedia's 40.6833, -74.4003 differs by roughly 600 metres and the discrepancy is recorded in the report.
stops.campa: Ritchie joins the Computing Science Research Center at Bell Telephone Laboratories, 600 Mountain Avenue, Murray Hill. His father has worked for the company for decades. The building is a mile of corridor with laboratories opening off both sides, laid out so that a man walking to lunch must pass the doors of people working on problems unlike his own. Ritchie will work inside it for forty years. The company that owns the address will be renamed three times; the address does not change.
suggested_refs: Bell Telephone Laboratories, 600 Mountain Avenue, Murray Hill, New Jersey

stops.name: Murray Hill, three years inside Multics
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: sources date Ritchie's Multics work only to 'the 1960s'. Month and day defaulted to 01. His personal presence at MIT's Project MAC, as against work done from Bell Labs terminals, is not confirmed by any source, so the stop is anchored at Murray Hill.
stops.campa: Bell Labs is one of three partners in Multics, with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and General Electric, building a time-sharing system on the GE 645 meant to sell computing the way the phone company sells dial tone. Ritchie works on it. The system is enormously ambitious and enormously late, and the lesson he takes from it is a negative one: the hierarchical file system and the shell are worth keeping, and nearly everything else is worth not building. He works from a terminal at Murray Hill, on a machine three hundred miles away.
suggested_refs: MIT Project MAC, 545 Technology Square, Cambridge, Massachusetts, centre of the Multics effort
The GE 645 and the Multics hierarchical file system

stops.name: Murray Hill, Bell Labs leaves the consortium
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Bell Labs withdraws from Multics, judging that the system is years from usable and that the company has bought nothing for its money. The machine goes back. What is left at Murray Hill is a group of researchers who have spent three years learning what a good time-sharing environment feels like to work in, and who now have no time-sharing environment at all. Nothing is entered on the books to replace the project. No manager approves what happens next.
suggested_refs: The Bell Labs withdrawal from the Multics consortium, 1969

stops.name: Murray Hill, the PDP-7 in the corner
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Thompson, deprived of the Multics machine, is left holding a game he wrote for it: Space Travel, which simulates the solar system and lets a player set a ship down on the planets. He moves it onto a discarded PDP-7 standing unused in a corner, and to make it run he has to write a file system, a scheduler, and a set of utilities. That is the operating system. Ritchie comes in early on the design and stays. Within two years neither man can say cleanly which parts are whose.
stops.quote: Thompson wanted to create a comfortable computing environment constructed according to his own design, using whatever means were available.
stops.quote_source: Dennis M. Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993), chist.html
suggested_refs: The DEC PDP-7 at Bell Labs Murray Hill, first machine to run Unix
Space Travel, Ken Thompson's solar-system game
sources: Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993)

stops.name: Murray Hill, B and the eight thousand bytes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01. Ritchie's own retrospective dates B to the PDP-7 period without a month.
stops.campa: Thompson needs a language above assembler for the PDP-7. He tries Fortran first and abandons it quickly. What he writes instead is B, a stripped descendant of Martin Richards's BCPL: typeless, taking the machine word rather than the character as its unit of storage, with generalized assignment operators written x=+y. It is small because the machine is small. Ritchie will spend the next three years putting back into it the things that eight thousand bytes of memory forced Thompson to leave out.
stops.quote: B can be thought of as C without types; more accurately, it is BCPL squeezed into 8K bytes of memory and filtered through Thompson's brain.
stops.quote_source: Dennis M. Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993), chist.html
suggested_refs: Martin Richards, BCPL, the ancestor language behind B and C
sources: Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993), fetched from chist.html

stops.name: Murray Hill, the name Unix
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Brian Kernighan, working down the corridor, proposes a name for the small system: Unix, a pun on Multics, one where the other was many. Multics was to be everything for everyone at once; the thing on the PDP-7 does one user's work at a time, with tools small enough to hold in the head. The name is never formally adopted by anything. It is simply what everyone in the building calls it, and then what everyone else calls it. Kernighan, who supplies the word, is not one of the system's authors.
suggested_refs: Brian W. Kernighan on the naming of Unix

stops.name: Murray Hill, the PDP-11 and the Unix Room
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The group acquires a PDP-11, the first machine bought for the project rather than salvaged, and moves the system onto it. Ritchie, Thompson, Rudd Canaday, Doug McIlroy, and Joe Ossanna work out of one shared laboratory room, which comes to be called the Unix Room and keeps that name in use for decades. Authorship inside the room is collective by default, and the two names most often attached to whatever leaves it are Thompson's and Ritchie's. Nobody keeps minutes.
stops.quote: By 1970, the Unix project had shown enough promise that we were able to acquire the new DEC PDP-11
stops.quote_source: Dennis M. Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993), chist.html; the fetched text may be truncated at this clause boundary
suggested_refs: The Unix Room at Bell Labs Murray Hill
The DEC PDP-11, the machine C was shaped by
sources: Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993)

stops.name: Murray Hill, New B and the byte
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The PDP-11 addresses bytes, and B, which knows only machine words, cannot reach them. Ritchie adds a character type and rewrites the compiler to exploit the new instruction set, calling the result New B. It is a repair, not a design. What the machine can do in a single instruction is what the language acquires a way of saying, and most of what is later praised or cursed in C enters it under that rule. No theory of languages is consulted at any point.
stops.quote: The advent of the PDP-11 exposed several inadequacies of B's semantic model.
stops.quote_source: Dennis M. Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993), chist.html
suggested_refs: The PDP-11 instruction set and byte addressing, the pressure that produced C
sources: Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993)

stops.name: Murray Hill, the language named C
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Ritchie adds arrays, pointers, structures, and typed function returns, writes a new compiler for the whole of it, and calls the language C, the next letter after B. The compiler is small enough that one person can hold the whole translation in his head, and Ritchie does. No committee reviews the design: a working programmer, on a machine in a room, adds what the operating system he is writing turns out to need, and stops when it is enough. C ships with the second edition of Unix.
stops.quote: C is quirky, flawed, and an enormous success.
stops.quote_source: Dennis M. Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993), chist.html
suggested_refs: The second edition of Unix, first release to carry a C compiler
sources: Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993)

stops.name: Yorktown Heights, the paper at the fourth SOSP
stops.date_confidence: attested: the fourth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles ran 15-17 October 1973 at the IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center. The research pool dated this presentation to 1974 and placed it at Bell Labs, conflating it with the Communications of the ACM publication of July 1974; corrected here.
stops.campa: Ritchie and Thompson travel north into New York State, to the IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center at Yorktown Heights, and present The UNIX Time-Sharing System at the fourth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles. It is the first full public account of the system outside Bell Labs, delivered inside a competitor's research laboratory. The paper is short and plain and claims very little for itself. It appears in Communications of the ACM the following July, and from that printing the system begins leaving the building.
stops.quote: The names of Ritchie and Thompson may safely be assumed to be attached to almost everything not otherwise attributed.
stops.quote_source: Doug McIlroy, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Ken Thompson'
suggested_refs: Ritchie and Thompson, 'The UNIX Time-Sharing System', Communications of the ACM 17(7), July 1974
IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, New York

stops.name: Murray Hill, the kernel rewritten in C
stops.date_confidence: attested for the month and year; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Ritchie and Thompson rewrite the entire Unix kernel in C. Operating systems are written in assembler because an operating system is the one program that has to know the machine exactly; writing one in a language above the metal is close to a category error at the time. It works. The system runs slower afterwards. What it gains is portability: the kernel becomes source that can be recompiled for a machine it was never written for, and the first port off DEC hardware follows within three years.
suggested_refs: The 1975 sale of the first Unix source licence to Donald B. Gillies at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, first academic consequence of the rewrite
The 1976-77 Interdata 7/32 port of Version 6 at the University of Wollongong, New South Wales, first port to non-DEC hardware

segments.name: Books, Ports, and the Paper That Was Not Published

stops.name: Murray Hill, Unix carried onto the Interdata 8/32
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the work is usually given as 1977-1978. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Ritchie ports Version 7 Unix in-house to the Interdata 8/32, a machine with nothing in common with the PDP-11 the system grew up on. The port is the proof of the 1973 rewrite: what was written for one manufacturer's instruction set comes up on another's. The same demonstration is made independently at the University of Wollongong in New South Wales, on an Interdata 7/32, from the same source, ten thousand miles from Mountain Avenue and without help from it.
suggested_refs: The Interdata 8/32 port of Version 7 Unix, done at Bell Labs
The University of Wollongong Interdata 7/32 port of Version 6, 1976-77

stops.name: Murray Hill, the M-209 and the National Security Agency
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the date: Wikipedia places the Reeds, Morris and Ritchie work on the M-209 in 'the 1970s'; the unpublished paper is dated 1978. Month and day defaulted to 01. The research pool called the M-209 a German wartime machine and said the work was published; it was an American army machine and the work was never published.
stops.campa: With James Reeds and Robert Morris, Ritchie works out a ciphertext-only attack on the M-209, the American army's field cipher machine of the Second World War, a Hagelin design still in service in other countries. The three of them write it up. After discussions with the National Security Agency the paper is not published, and it stays unpublished. The only account of the work anywhere in the public record is Ritchie's own later description of why it was withheld.
stops.quote: after discussions with the National Security Agency, the authors decided not to publish it, as they were told that the principle applied to machines still in use by foreign governments.
stops.quote_source: Dennis Ritchie, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Dennis Ritchie'
suggested_refs: The Hagelin M-209, US Army field cipher machine of the Second World War
Robert Morris and James Reeds, Bell Labs cryptography group

stops.name: Englewood Cliffs, Prentice Hall publishes K and R
stops.date_confidence: attested for the full date. Coordinates corrected to the borough of Englewood Cliffs; the research pool's value fell in the Hudson River, some 2.7 km west.
stops.campa: Prentice Hall publishes The C Programming Language by Brian W. Kernighan and Dennis M. Ritchie, from its offices at Englewood Cliffs on the Palisades above the Hudson. It is a thin book. For the next eleven years it is the only definition of the language there is: no standard exists, and what the book says C does is what C does. Byte magazine, reviewing it in 1983, calls it the definitive work on the C language. Its first example program prints the words hello, world.
stops.quote: The rule, which survives in today's C, is that values of array type are converted, when they appear in expressions, into pointers to the first of the objects making up the array.
stops.quote_source: Dennis M. Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993), chist.html
suggested_refs: The C Programming Language, first edition, Prentice Hall, 22 February 1978
Byte magazine review, August 1983, calling it 'the definitive work on the C language'

stops.name: Murray Hill, Version 7 and the arrival of Stroustrup
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the Version 7 release and of Stroustrup's arrival at Murray Hill (1 April 1979). Month and day defaulted to 01 for the release.
stops.campa: Version 7 Unix ships, the last Research Unix release before AT&T begins treating the system as a product to be licensed rather than a paper to be sent out. The same year a Danish computer scientist named Bjarne Stroustrup arrives at Murray Hill to work on Unix kernels, finds C in the building and Simula's classes in his memory of Aarhus, and by October is writing a preprocessor that adds one to the other. The preprocessor emits C, which Ritchie's own compiler then translates. Ritchie is down the corridor.
suggested_refs: Bjarne Stroustrup's Cpre preprocessor, October 1979, later C with Classes and then C++
Stroustrup, 'Classes: An Abstract Data Type Facility for the C Language' (1982)
sources: bjarne_stroustrup.journey.json, stops 'Murray Hill, arrival at Bell Laboratories' and 'Murray Hill, the Cpre preprocessor'

segments.name: The Honors, and the Language Made a Standard

stops.name: Murray Hill, the Piore Award
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01. No ceremony venue is named in any source consulted, so the stop is anchored where Ritchie worked.
stops.campa: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers gives Ritchie the Emanuel R. Piore Award, for contributions to the field of information processing. It is the first of the major honors and among the least remembered of them. By this point Unix runs in most computer science departments in the United States, and the C compiler travels with it. A generation of students is learning to program in a language written by a man they have never heard of. Nothing on the screen in front of them carries his name.
suggested_refs: The IEEE Emanuel R. Piore Award, 1982

stops.name: Murray Hill, the Turing Award
stops.date_confidence: the award and its year are firmly attested; the ceremony venue is not. No source consulted names it. The research pool supplied a placeholder coordinate that turned out to be the Empire State Building, never an ACM address; it has been dropped rather than replaced, and the stop is anchored at Murray Hill.
stops.campa: The Association for Computing Machinery gives the A.M. Turing Award jointly to Ritchie and Thompson, for their development of generic operating systems theory and specifically for the implementation of the UNIX operating system. It is the field's highest honor, given for a system begun on a discarded machine so that a game could be played on it. Neither man is comfortable with the founder's role the citation confers, and Ritchie is said to have refused it in one sentence.
stops.quote: I am not now, nor have I ever been, a member of the demigodic party.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Dennis Ritchie via Wikiquote; not traced to any primary Ritchie document in this research, and carried as reconstruction
suggested_refs: Ritchie's Turing lecture, 'Reflections on Software Research', Communications of the ACM, August 1984

stops.name: Murray Hill, the second and last edition of the book
stops.date_confidence: attested for month and year; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Kernighan and Ritchie issue the second edition of The C Programming Language, revised to the draft ANSI standard. It is the last edition either man will ever publish. The book is translated into more than twenty languages and stays in print, unrevised, for decades after the language it describes has been standardized twice more and extended in directions neither author would have chosen. The prose is not revised either. It reads in the 2012 ebook editions exactly as it read in April 1988.
suggested_refs: The C Programming Language, second edition, Prentice Hall, April 1988
The 2012 ebook editions in ePub, Mobi and PDF

stops.name: Murray Hill, C ratified as a standard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the American national standard, ANSI X3.159-1989; month and day defaulted to 01. The international adoption as ISO/IEC 9899:1990 came the following year. The research pool conflated the two into a single 1989 ISO ratification.
stops.campa: C is ratified as an American national standard, ANSI X3.159-1989, and adopted internationally the year after as ISO/IEC 9899:1990. The language Ritchie wrote by himself for one PDP-11 now has a committee behind it, a formal document, and a definition of what it means to conform. Standardization changes almost nothing about the language and everything about who is permitted to say what it is. Linus Torvalds, a student in Helsinki, learns C out of that standard.
stops.quote: C remains a simple and small language, translatable with simple and small compilers.
stops.quote_source: Dennis M. Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (HOPL II, 1993), chist.html
suggested_refs: ANSI X3.159-1989 and ISO/IEC 9899:1990
linus_torvalds.journey.json, stop on the university DEC MicroVAX running ULTRIX and the reading of the C standard

stops.name: Murray Hill, the Hamming Medal
stops.date_confidence: the award and year are attested; the ceremony venue is not, and the research pool's coordinate for it was the same non-IEEE placeholder used for the Turing entry. Anchored at Murray Hill; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The IEEE awards Ritchie and Thompson the Richard W. Hamming Medal, for the origination of the Unix operating system and the C programming language. It is the second joint award in seven years, and it will not be the last. From here the honors arrive at intervals, always jointly, always naming the two of them in the same order, always for the same two objects. Ritchie mentions almost none of them in his own writing. What he is writing, by 1990, is manual pages and one history of a language.
suggested_refs: The IEEE Richard W. Hamming Medal, 1990

stops.name: Murray Hill, named a Computer Pioneer
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01. No ceremony venue is named in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The IEEE Computer Society names Ritchie a Computer Pioneer. The category is retrospective by design, awarded for work whose consequences have settled, and by 1994 the consequences of Unix and C are past arguing about: the operating system runs the machines carrying the early internet, and the language is what compilers, kernels, and other languages are written in. Ritchie is fifty-two, still working in the same building, on a system intended to replace the one being honored.
suggested_refs: The IEEE Computer Society Computer Pioneer Award, 1994

segments.name: Plan 9, Inferno, and the Change of Owners

stops.name: Murray Hill, Plan 9 from Bell Labs
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: sources date Ritchie's Plan 9 work only to 'the 1980s and 1990s'. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Plan 9 from Bell Labs takes the Unix idea further than Unix took it. Ritchie is among its leaders, alongside Thompson, Rob Pike, and others out of the same room. By most of the measures its authors care about it is a better design than Unix, and it displaces Unix nowhere: the world has already been built on the earlier thing. What Plan 9 proposes instead is that every resource be a file, that every process carry a namespace of its own, and that a network of machines present itself to a user as one system.
suggested_refs: Plan 9 from Bell Labs, the successor research system

stops.name: Murray Hill, Inferno and Limbo
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: sources date the Inferno and Limbo work only to 'the 1990s'. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Plan 9 line continues into Inferno, a distributed operating system meant to run on anything from a set-top box to a workstation, and into Limbo, the language written for it. Ritchie contributes to both. It is the third time he has done the same thing: a system, a language written to implement that system, and the two designed against each other until neither can be lifted out. Unix and C escaped the building. Plan 9, Inferno, and Limbo did not.
suggested_refs: The Inferno operating system and the Limbo programming language, Bell Labs

stops.name: Murray Hill, the Labs change owners
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: AT&T splits itself into three companies, and Bell Labs goes with the equipment business into the new Lucent Technologies. The institution that once funded a research center where a man could spend a year writing a compiler nobody had asked for is now a listed company answerable to quarterly results. The arrangement that produced Unix ends quietly, around the people who had benefited from it. Ritchie's group changes letterhead. He does not change desks.
suggested_refs: The 1996 AT&T trivestiture and the creation of Lucent Technologies

stops.name: Murray Hill, Fellow of the Computer History Museum
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01. No source places Ritchie at any induction event in California, so the stop is anchored at Murray Hill.
stops.campa: The Computer History Museum elects Ritchie a Fellow for the co-creation of the Unix operating system and the C programming language. The museum stands three thousand miles from Murray Hill and collects the machines his software outlived: the PDP-7 the system was begun on, the PDP-11 the language was shaped by. Twenty-three years later the same institution will catalogue the Harvard dissertation he never turned into a degree, and put it where anyone can read it.
suggested_refs: Computer History Museum Fellow Awards, 1997
Computer History Museum catalogue record 102784979, Ritchie's copy of his 1968 thesis

stops.name: The White House, the National Medal of Technology
stops.date_confidence: attested for the full date of the ceremony; the medal itself belongs to the 1998 award year, presented the following spring in the Medal's usual pattern.
stops.campa: Ritchie and Thompson travel to Washington, and President Bill Clinton hangs the National Medal of Technology on them at a White House ceremony, for the 1998 award year. It is the highest technological honor the United States gives. Both men are in their fifties. Both have spent their whole working lives at the same company, in the same building, and neither has worked anywhere else. The citation names the operating system and the language, and then the hardware, software, and networking systems that other people built on them over thirty years.
stops.quote: For co-inventing the UNIX operating system and the C programming language which together have led to enormous advances in computer hardware, software, and networking systems.
stops.quote_source: National Medal of Technology citation, 1998 award year, presented 21 April 1999
suggested_refs: The National Medal of Technology and Innovation, 1998 award year
sources: Wikipedia, 'National Medal of Technology and Innovation'

stops.name: Murray Hill, head of System Software Research
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: sources give only 'early 2000s' for the appointment. Month, day and year defaulted.
stops.campa: Ritchie is head of the System Software Research Department at Bell Labs, which is what the group that built Unix has become after several rounds of reorganization and one change of owner. He manages research inside an industrial laboratory that no longer has much appetite for the unsupervised kind that made his own career. He answers mail from strangers about C, patiently, for years, and keeps a personal page on the Bell Labs server with the history of the language on it.
suggested_refs: Ritchie's Bell Labs home page, host of 'The Development of the C Language' (chist.html)

stops.name: Murray Hill, the late awards
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years of both awards, 2003 and 2005; month and day defaulted to 01. Neither has an attested ceremony venue, so the stop is anchored at Murray Hill.
stops.campa: The University of Pennsylvania gives Ritchie the Harold Pender Award; two years later the Industrial Research Institute gives him its Achievement Award. He is sixty-two, then sixty-four. stops.name: Murray Hill, forty years and out
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Ritchie retires from Alcatel-Lucent Bell Labs as head of the System Software Research Department, forty years after walking into the Computing Science Research Center out of Harvard. He arrived when the Labs were a monopoly's research arm with money and patience; he leaves them a division of a French telecommunications manufacturer. The Computing Science Research Center he walked into no longer exists under that name. He worked in one building for the whole of his adult life. Ken Thompson had gone seven years earlier.

stops.name: Berkeley Heights, the house four miles west
stops.date_confidence: attested that he lived alone in Berkeley Heights; the address was never made public, so the township centroid is the anchor and the research pool's more precise-looking point has been dropped. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Ritchie lives alone in Berkeley Heights, the next township west, a few miles from the Mountain Avenue building. He never married and has no children. Those who knew him describe a man who reads science fiction and listens to classical music and answers questions about pointer arithmetic from people with no idea who he is. The drive from this house to the desk he worked at for forty years takes under ten minutes. He keeps his page on the Bell Labs server up, and the mail from strangers keeps arriving. He is sixty-six.

stops.campa: The Japan Prize Foundation names Ritchie and Thompson laureates in Information and Communications, with a citation of eight words: Development of the operating system, UNIX. It is the last honor the two receive together, and the first from outside the Western technical world. Ritchie is sixty-nine, has been treated for prostate cancer and for heart disease, and has been in frail health for several years. Their two names have now been paired in citations for twenty-eight years.

stops.name: Berkeley Heights, found at home
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date of discovery; he died at home over the preceding weekend, c. 8-9 October. The research pool's claim that the death was reported 'a week later' is wrong and appears to have borrowed the Steve Jobs interval; Pike's post went up the same day.
stops.campa: Ritchie is found dead at his home in Berkeley Heights, seventy years old, having died over the preceding weekend. The cause is never made public. Rob Pike, who worked beside him at Murray Hill for decades, posts the news that same day on Google+, and it is the first anyone outside the family hears of it. The post is a few lines long, and the platform carrying it will later be shut down. Alcatel-Lucent issues nothing. Steve Jobs had died seven days earlier.
stops.quote: I just heard that, after a long illness, Dennis Ritchie (dmr) died at home this weekend.
stops.quote_source: Rob Pike, Google+ post, 12 October 2011, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Dennis Ritchie'

stops.campa: Fedora 16 is released on 8 November, four weeks after his death, and dedicated to his memory. FreeBSD 9.0 follows on 12 January, dedicated in the same terms, from the other side of the Unix family split that AT&T's licensing had opened. In February the Minor Planet Center publishes the citation for asteroid 294727, found in 2008 by Tom Glinos and David H. Levy and now named Dennisritchie. No grave, headstone, or memorial site for him appears in any accessible record.

stops.name: Murray Hill, the corridor under new owners
stops.date_confidence: no single date attaches to this; the stop records the state of the site after his death and the year is a placeholder set to the January following it.
stops.campa: Six hundred Mountain Avenue is still a working research site, under Nokia Bell Labs, the fourth owner of the corridor Ritchie walked for forty years. Sections of the original building have been demolished. Brian Kernighan, who wrote the book with him, says the tools Dennis built and their direct descendants run pretty much everything today. The historian Paul Ceruzzi states the same fact from the other end, from outside the field, where the name had never arrived at all.
stops.quote: His name was not a household name at all, but if you had a microscope and could look in a computer, you'd see his work everywhere inside.
stops.quote_source: Paul E. Ceruzzi, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Dennis Ritchie'
